title: The Last Buna
audience: Ethiopians, especially young adults living away from their families, and viewers abroad who are curious about Ethiopian life. Watched on a phone, on YouTube, Reels or TikTok.
feeling: Love and longing for a parent: however far you go, do not forget the person who is waiting for you at home.
story:
This is a made-up story. Its people are invented and are not real.

In the city of Jimma, in the green coffee hills of south-west Ethiopia, a widow named Emaye Zewditu lives in a small house with a tin roof and a blue wooden door. Every morning before sunrise she spreads fresh green grass on the floor and lights a charcoal stove. She washes green coffee beans in a bowl and roasts them on a flat iron pan until they turn dark and shine. She carries the smoking pan around the room so the smell fills the house. She pounds the beans in a wooden mortar and boils them in a black clay jebena. She burns frankincense beside the cups.

In Jimma, coffee is poured three times. The first cup is called abol. The second is called tona. The third and last cup is called baraka, which means blessing.

Her only son, Dawit, left Jimma seven years ago on a bus to Addis Ababa to find work. On the day he left, she told him the third cup would always be his. Since then she has set two small white cups on the tray every morning, and a low wooden stool beside the door. She drinks the first cup and the second cup. She pours the third cup for Dawit and leaves it on the tray. Every evening the third cup is cold, and she pours it onto the roots of the coffee tree in her yard.

Dawit works in a tall building in Addis Ababa. He calls on holidays. He always says he will come next year.

One morning in the rainy season, the blue door opens before the coffee has boiled. Dawit is standing there with a dusty bag. He sits on the low stool. That morning he pours the third cup himself, and he gives it to his mother.
